title: Chapter 29: The Morning Dew 2
content:
Chapter 29

"Hold your horses, I was just getting to that," the server said, waving a greasy hand. "Theydidall die. When I said he dodged a blade, I meant temporarily. A few years down the line, Master Chang Ping got his turn. And let me tell you, that death was ten times more gruesome—hacked to pieces with a sword, executed by lingering slicing! Slicing by a thousand cuts—lingchi! Need I spell that out? It’s taking a blade and peeling a man's flesh away, stroke by stroke, three thousand six hundred times until the meat falls clean off the bone..."

Naturally, Wei Wuxian needed no lecture on the finer mechanics oflingchi. If anyone on earth were qualified to pen a comprehensive encyclopedia titledA Thousand Ways to Die Horribly, he would easily claim author credits.

Raising a casual palm, he interjected, "Right, crystal clear. Tell me, brother: do you knowwhythe Chang Clan got butchered in the first place?"

"Word on the street says they got set up by their own kind," the server muttered conspiratorially. "Stands to reason, doesn't it? Otherwise, how could a whole pack of living, breathing cultivators fail to hop a wall? Someone—or something—must have trapped them inside."

Worrying the table's conversation might dry up, the proprietor hurried over with two complimentary saucers of roasted peanuts and melon seeds. Wei Wuxian nodded his thanks, casually cracking a seed between his teeth as he pressed, "Did anyone ever figure out who—or what—pulled it off?"

The boy barked a laugh. "You're pulling my leg, Young Master! How would an ordinary street peddler scraping together coppers know the high-and-mighty affairs of immortals riding the clouds? By rights, you're a cultivator yourself—you ought to know better than me! All I caught wind of was that they crossed someone they had no business crossing. Ever since, this whole stretch of Yueyang has been an open buffet for ghosts and ghouls. Not a single soul left to clean them out."

Wei Wuxian mulled it over. "Someone they had no business crossing?"

"You bet." The server tossed a pair of peanuts into his mouth. "The bad blood between these grand clans runs deep. My guess? Some rival sect set their sights on the Changs. Murder someone to rob their treasures—it happens all the time! That's what the storytellers say at the tea houses, and that's how it's written in the penny dreadfuls. I don't know the exact name, but word is, it traces back to some notorious fiend."

Wei Wuxian brought his wine bowl to his lips, eye curving with amused suspicion. "Let me guess. You're about to tell me you don't know who this notorious fiend is, right?"

The boy grinned broadly. "Wrong! I actually know this one! Called himself some kind of Old Monster... No, wait—Patriarch! The Yiling Patriarch!"

Wei Wuxian choked on his swallow, blowing an undignified volley of bubbles right into his wine bowl. "Come again?!"

Him?! Again?!

The server gave a definitive nod. "Yep, that’s the bastard! Surname Wei, something like Wei Wuqian! Whenever folks bring him up, they sound downright sick with dread and spit venom!" (A/n- Wuqian 无钱 means penniless)

Wei Wuxian sat in stony silence.

Running through the mental archives of his past life, he was dead certain of two indisputable facts: first, he had never set foot in Yueyang in his life; second, out of every single soul he had ever put in the ground, not a single one had met their end by death by a thousand cuts. The absurdity was staggering.

He craned his neck toward Lan Wangji, wordlessly demanding a reality check.

Lan Wangji had apparently been waiting for that exact glance. Setting down his cup, he uttered a single, clipped word: "Leave."

Wei Wuxian caught the drift instantly. Lan Wangji had something to say, and it wasn't the sort of business you aired over cheap wine in a bustling tavern.

Pushing his stool back, Wei Wuxian rose. "Right, time to hit the road. The tab... paid already, excellent. Brother, stash the rest of those jars for us behind the counter. We’ll be back for a refill once our errand wraps up." He flashed a playful grin. "No dipping your hand into our supply, mind you."

Having devoured half the peanuts, the server piped up, "Perish the thought! Honest business under this roof, guaranteed! Leave 'em right here—we won't shutter the gates until you return. Say, are you two heading toward the Chang estate right now? Whew, talk about guts! Even as a local, I've never had the stomach to set foot near it—only ever caught glimpses from a safe distance down the road. Are you really going inside? What's the plan?"

Wei Wuxian chuckled softly. "We're just going to sneak a peek. From a very, very safe distance."

The young server was a shameless chatterbox who clearly never met a stranger. Sensing camaraderie, he leaned in close, raising an arm to throw it over Wei Wuxian's shoulder. "Is that line of work brutal? Does it pay well? Must be rolling in silver, right? So respectable! Tell me, is the entry exam tough? Can someone like me—"

His rambling came to a dead halt. The boy flinched, shrinking back as his eyes darted toward the other side of the table. "Young Master..." he whispered nervously, "why is your friend over there... glaring at me like he wants my head on a spike?"

Wei Wuxian followed his gaze, catching Lan Wangji rising from his seat and pivoting cleanly toward the threshold.

"Oh, him?" Wei Wuxian chuckled. "He was raised under an absurdly strict household. Hates seeing folks get touchy-feely in his presence. A bit eccentric, wouldn't you say?"

The server hastily tucked his hands behind his back, muttering under his breath, "Eccentric is putting it mildly. Look at that glare... anyone would think I just put my arm around his wife..."

With Lan Wangji's frighteningly sharp spiritual senses, lowering one's voice meant nothing; the muttered comment had undoubtedly hit its mark, leaving Wei Wuxian privately wondering how the pristine Hanguang-jun was processing that one. Swallowing a belly laugh so hard it practically bruised his ribs, Wei Wuxian turned back to the boy, clapping a hand to his own chest. "Well, I finished the jar."

The server blinked. "Huh?"

Wei Wuxian pointed at his own feet. "Still on two legs."

The boy finally remembered his earlier boast—If you're still standing after a bowl, I'll take your family name!

"Oh! Oh, damn!" the boy sputtered, clearly impressed. "Color me shocked! Truth be told, that’s the very first time I’ve seen someone knock back a full jar and stay on their feet without their tongue tangling up! What’s your noble surname, sir?"

"Mine?" Wei Wuxian began. Catching the memory of that ridiculous 'Wei-Without-a-Penny' crack, the corner of his mouth twitched. With utter serenity, he smoothly replied, "Lan."

The server didn't miss a beat. Grinning shamelessly, he puffed out his chest and declared at the top of his lungs, "Done! From this day forth, my name is Lan!"

Under the bright red banner flapping in the breeze, Lan Wangji's immaculate, snow-white silhouette seemed to falter by the barest fraction of an inch.

Grinning from ear to ear, Wei Wuxian strolled forward with his hands clasped behind his back, giving the man's shoulder an affectionate slap. "My humble thanks to Hanguang-jun for covering the tab. I've taken the liberty of adopting him into your clan."

Leaving the city walls behind, the two followed the road the server had pointed out. The bustle of travelers dwindled away, replaced by the quiet rustle of thickening roadside timber.

Wei Wuxian broke the silence. "Why cut me off back there?"

"I recalled the tragedy of the Yueyang Chang Clan," Lan Wangji answered evenly. "There was no need to probe further."

Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin. "Before you spill the details, let me get a quick reality check. You can vouch for me on this, right? The slaughter of the Chang Clan wasn't my doing?"

Leaving aside the inconvenient detail that he’d been dead for a decade, his soul had spent those years lying dormant; it was mathematically impossible for him to have massacred an entire household and somehow blanked on the memory.

"It was not you," Lan Wangji replied.

"Good to know," Wei Wuxian sighed. For a fleeting second, it felt as though he’d tumbled straight back into his previous life—the dark, pariah years when he was treated worse than a gutter rat, where every ill omen under heaven was laid squarely at his doorstep. If an old neighbor's grandchild skipped dinner and dropped half a pound, the townsfolk would undoubtedly claim the child had been scared sick by tavern horror stories of the Yiling Patriarch siccing the Ghost General.

"It was not your hand," Lan Wangji added quietly, "yet it is tied to you."

Wei Wuxian paused. "How so?"

"In two ways," Lan Wangji said. "First: an individual involved in the affair shares deep ties with your mother."

Wei Wuxian’s boots froze against the dirt path.

A strange, unnamable tangle knotted in his chest. His face went entirely blank, his voice dipping into uncertain hesitation: "...My mother?"

Wei Wuxian was the son of Wei Changze, a loyal servant of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan, and Cangse Sanren, a wandering rogue cultivator. Jiang Fengmian and his wife had known his parents intimately, but Sect Leader Jiang rarely reminisced about his departed friends. As for Madam Yu, Yu Ziyuan, she had never spared him a civil breath in her life; if she wasn't threatening to break out Zidian or ordering him to kneel in the ancestral hall and keep his distance from Jiang Cheng, it was considered a mild day. Most of what Wei Wuxian knew of his parents had been pieced together from scattered gossip; truthfully, he knew little more than an outsider.

Lan Wangji halted as well, turning to meet his gaze. "Have you ever heard the name Xiao Xingchen?"

Wei Wuxian searched his memories, then shook his head. "Never."

"It stands to reason," Lan Wangji said. "He descended the mountain and made his name twelve years ago. Few speak of him today."

Twelve years ago—barely a year after the siege of the Burial Mounds. They had missed each other by a hair's breadth.

"Which mountain?" Wei Wuxian asked. "Whose lineage?"

"The mountain is unknown," Lan Wangji replied. "His lineage belongs to the Daoist path. Xiao Xingchen was a disciple of Baoshan Sanren."

The puzzle pieces fell into place.

"So," Wei Wuxian murmured, "this Xiao Xingchen would technically be my martial uncle."

Cangse Sanren had trained under the very same master.

Baoshan Sanren was a legendary hermit who had roamed the realm alongside the likes of Wen Mao and Lan An during the genesis of the cultivation world. The titans of that glorious era had long since dissolved into dust, yet rumors insisted that Baoshan Sanren had never perished. If true, she would be hundreds of years old—a staggering testament to her transcendent cultivation.

Back when Wen Mao led the shift toward clan-based dynasties over loose sects, cultivating lineages bound by blood had sprouted across the land like bamboo shoots after rain. Any cultivator with a scrap of renown had rushed to carve out a family name and plant their flag. Yet this extraordinary cultivator had chosen total withdrawal, retreating into the deep mists with the titleBaoshan—she who cradles the mountain.

Which mountain she embraced, no mortal knew. Then again, that was the entire point of a hermit's retreat; if a sacred sanctuary could be tracked down with a map, it hardly deserved the name.

Perched atop her celestial peak, she would occasionally take pity on destitute orphans, carrying them up the mountain to instruct them in the Dao. Yet every disciple had to swear a binding oath upon initiation:Devote yourself entirely to the pursuit of the Dao; never descend the mountain, never set foot in the mortal coil. Should you break this decree for any reason, you shall never return. You must make your own way through the red dust, utterly severed from your master's lineage.

Generations of scholars praised Baoshan Sanren’s mandate as profound foresight. Across hundreds of years, only three pupils had ever dared descend from her mists: Yanling Daoren, Cangse Sanren, and Xiao Xingchen.

And not a single one had met a peaceful end.

The fates of the first two were tragedies Wei Wuxian had grown up hearing, etched deep into his heart. So Lan Wangji kept his account brief, outlining the legend of this final martial uncle.

Xiao Xingchen had stepped into the mortal realm at the tender age of seventeen. Though Lan Wangji had never crossed paths with the man in the flesh, he had heard endless praise of his striking grace from those who had.

At the time, the dust from the Sunshot Campaign had barely settled, and the hysteria following the siege of the Burial Mounds was still raw. The great clans were aggressively consolidating power, combing the four corners of the land to recruit rogue talent into their ranks. Driven by an earnest desire to bring salvation to the world, Xiao Xingchen descended from the mountain—brilliantly gifted, trained under a legendary immortal. On his maiden night-hunt, armed with nothing more than a horsetail whisk and a slender longsword, he breached a haunted peak entirely alone and claimed the prize in a single stroke.

A legend was born overnight.

Enamored by his pristine virtue and peerless martial skill, the prominent clans scrambled to shower the young Daoist with invitations. Yet Xiao Xingchen politely declined every single overture, explicitly stating he had no intention of bending the knee to any aristocratic family. Instead, alongside a kindred spirit, his singular dream was to establish a brand-new sect—one unbound by bloodlines or nepotism.

He was gentle as a reed yet unyielding as granite—soft on the outside, steel at the core, maintaining an immaculate moral compass. Whenever commoners or wandering cultivators ran into an impossible horror, Xiao Xingchen was the very first name on their lips; and because he never turned a plea away, his reputation was universally revered.

And it was during that brilliant era that the tragedy of the Yueyang Chang Clan came to pass.
